sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pneumonia?
sections.body:
The NHS says pneumonia symptoms can come on suddenly or build up over a few days. A cough, breathlessness and a fever are typical, and chest pain and confusion can also occur, with confusion being common in older people. Some people cough up yellow or green phlegm. Where the lining around the lung is also inflamed (pleurisy), the chest pain can be sharp and get worse when breathing.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness. It advises calling 999 for severe difficulty breathing, blue or pale skin or lips, coughing up blood or sudden confusion, and says not to drive yourself to A&E. Pneumonia is more common, and can be more serious, in young children.

sections.heading: What causes pneumonia, and what are the complications?
sections.body:
Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs. Bacteria, viruses or fungi can cause it. The NHS describes the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, also called pneumococcus, as a common bacterial cause, and the vaccines used against it are described below.

Aspiration, which means food or water going down into the lungs by mistake, can also trigger pneumonia, according to the sources reviewed.

Pneumonia can affect people of any age. The outlook for otherwise healthy people is good, but serious complications are more likely in the very young, the very old and people with another serious health condition.

Pneumonia can lead to serious complications, including a collection of pus around the lung (empyema), sepsis, respiratory failure and lung abscess. These are uncommon in healthy people.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets describe a doctor first asking about symptoms and examining the chest. A chest X-ray may be arranged to confirm the diagnosis, and blood tests and tests on a sample of phlegm (sputum) may also be done.

One purpose of the assessment is to judge how unwell the person is. NHS inform describes a scoring system called CRB-65 that estimates the risk of complications and whether urgent hospital treatment is needed. Most people recover at home, while people who are very unwell or at higher risk may be admitted.

In hospital the team can give antibiotics through a drip, and sometimes steroids, and may add oxygen to help breathing. The NHS says a follow-up chest X-ray is not routine for everyone. It may be arranged if symptoms have not improved or have come back, or if the person smokes or is over 50.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia treated, and how long does recovery take?
sections.body:
The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause. Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, plenty of rest and plenty of fluids. Pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics.

People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital. There the usual treatment is antibiotics, often given into a vein, and sometimes steroids. Oxygen can be added to help with breathing.

Recovery varies from person to person. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline: the high temperature should have gone after about a week, chest pain and mucus should have reduced substantially after about four weeks, and cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks. Most symptoms should have resolved by three months, although tiredness can linger, and most people feel back to normal by about six months.

Other NHS sources give a wider range, from a few weeks to several months. The cough may last for two to three weeks after the antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer as the body recovers. People who have had pneumonia are also more prone to other chest infections for a while.

sections.heading: Can pneumonia be prevented?
sections.body:
Vaccination lowers the risk of severe pneumonia, but it does not cover every cause. The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against serious pneumococcal infections, which can lead to pneumonia, septicaemia and meningitis.

In the UK the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is given to all children under two as part of the childhood programme. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is given to people aged 65 and over and to people at high risk because of long-term health conditions. The NHS also recommends flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines for specific groups, and an NHS Wales leaflet says that immunising children, including with the flu vaccine, reduces their risk of pneumonia.

faqs.q: Do all cases of pneumonia need antibiotics?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause, but pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics. The clinician judges the likely cause from the symptoms, examination and any tests, and decides on treatment accordingly.

faqs.q: Can pneumonia be treated at home?
faqs.a: Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, rest and plenty of fluids. People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital, where antibiotics are often given into a vein and oxygen can be added.

faqs.q: Why does the cough last so long after pneumonia?
faqs.a: The NHS and hospital leaflets say a cough can carry on for two to three weeks after antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline in which cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks.

faqs.q: When is pneumonia an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing, blue or pale skin or lips, coughing up blood or sudden confusion, and not to drive to A&E. For a cough, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness it advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine against pneumonia?
faqs.a: There are vaccines against some causes. The pneumococcal vaccine is given to all children under two and to people aged 65 and over or at high risk. Flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines are also advised for specific groups, but vaccines do not cover every cause of pneumonia.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS lists chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, pain that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, pale or grey skin and passing out as reasons to call 999 immediately. A heart attack is a medical emergency.

Not everyone has the classic chest pain. NHS 111 Wales notes that women are more likely to have other symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling or being sick, and back or jaw pain. The evidence on differences between men and women is mixed: a study funded by the British Heart Foundation (BHF) found that women having a heart attack reported the same key symptoms as men. Other guidance says symptoms can be less typical, particularly in women, older people and people with diabetes.

The NHS advises that, while waiting for the ambulance, a person who is not allergic to aspirin may chew and swallow an aspirin tablet.

sections.heading: What causes a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says a heart attack happens when the blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly cut off, so that the heart muscle begins to die. Coronary heart disease is the leading cause. In coronary heart disease, fatty plaques build up in the coronary arteries, and a plaque can rupture and trigger a clot that blocks the vessel. A shortage of oxygen in the blood, for example from carbon monoxide poisoning or lung problems, is a less common cause.

The NHS lists smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, being overweight and a close relative who has had a heart attack among the risk factors. Age, sex, family history and ethnicity are factors that cannot be changed.

A heart attack is a problem with the blood supply to the heart muscle. Cardiac arrest is different: the NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged, the heart can stop beating altogether.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main tests for finding out whether someone is having a heart attack are an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests.

There are two main types. In a STEMI, one of the coronary arteries is completely blocked, and the ECG usually shows a rise in a part of the tracing called the ST segment. In an NSTEMI, an artery is significantly narrowed rather than fully blocked, and the ECG often shows no abnormality or only subtle changes.

Damage to the heart muscle lets proteins leak into the blood. The most commonly measured is cardiac troponin, and the level helps diagnose the type of heart attack. A BHF briefing reports that a high-sensitivity troponin test can double the number of women diagnosed with a heart attack who would otherwise have been told they did not have one.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack treated?
sections.body:
Hospital treatment depends on the type and severity of the heart attack. The NHS lists clot-dissolving medicine, coronary angioplasty with one or more stents, and coronary artery bypass surgery. Angioplasty puts stents into the narrowed or blocked artery to hold it open.

For a STEMI, the usual approach is to offer a coronary angiogram, which images the arteries, followed by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (primary PCI), meaning emergency angioplasty, when symptoms began recently enough for it to help. NICE guideline NG185 covers the early management of acute coronary syndromes.

The NHS says people usually stay in hospital for about 2 to 5 days after a heart attack, and for 2 or 3 days if they have had angioplasty or stents.

The most common complications are abnormal heart rhythms (arrhythmias) and heart failure. Cardiogenic shock and rupture of the heart muscle are more serious but less common. How well someone does depends on age, how much heart muscle was damaged and how quickly treatment began.

sections.heading: What happens after a heart attack?
sections.body:
Most people are prescribed several medicines to lower the chance of another heart attack. The BHF says antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common, and a glyceryl trinitrate spray can ease chest pain.

The NHS says people are offered cardiac rehabilitation, which can be done in person or remotely. The BHF describes it as an exercise and education programme, with expert guidance, exercise sessions and regular assessments. It says programmes usually start two to six weeks after leaving hospital and can cover practical matters such as driving, returning to work and holidays.

The NHS says it can take around 4 to 6 weeks to return to work after a heart attack, and 6 to 8 weeks after a moderate or major one. A GP can provide a fit note if someone is not fit for work.

sections.heading: Feelings, anxiety and sex after a heart attack
sections.body:
An NHS cardiac rehabilitation guide says that having a heart attack is bound to lead to feelings of apprehension. The BHF says rehabilitation should include support for wellbeing, including an assessment of anxiety or depression, tips for dealing with stress and information on other sources of help.

The NHS says people can usually start having sex again once they feel well enough, often about 4 to 6 weeks after a heart attack, and that having sex does not put a person at further risk of another heart attack.

The BHF Heart Helpline offers advice and can help people find cardiac rehabilitation locally. Anyone who develops new chest pain, or the other warning signs described at the top of this article, should call 999 rather than wait.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
faqs.a: In a heart attack the blood supply to part of the heart muscle is suddenly cut off. In cardiac arrest the heart stops beating. The NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged in a heart attack, the heart can stop beating altogether.

faqs.q: Do women have different heart attack symptoms?
faqs.a: The evidence is mixed. A BHF-funded study found women report the same key symptoms as men, mainly chest pain. NHS 111 Wales notes women are more likely to have other symptoms too, such as breathlessness, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain.

faqs.q: How long do people stay in hospital?
faqs.a: The NHS says people usually stay in hospital for about 2 to 5 days after a heart attack. If they have had coronary angioplasty or stents, the stay is likely to be 2 or 3 days.

faqs.q: Will I need heart medicines for life?
faqs.a: The BHF says antiplatelets such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common. The clinical team decides which medicines each person needs.

faqs.q: When can I have sex again after a heart attack?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can usually start again once they feel well enough, usually about 4 to 6 weeks after a heart attack, and that sex does not put a person at further risk of another heart attack.

sections.heading: How is a DVT assessed in practice?
sections.body:
The NHS says that if a doctor thinks someone has a DVT, they should be referred to hospital within 24 hours for an ultrasound scan. The scan shows whether blood is flowing normally through the vein.

A hospital leaflet describes how the D-dimer blood test fits in. The doctor first estimates the likelihood of a clot using a points score called the Wells score. A low score combined with a negative D-dimer is enough to rule out a DVT, and no further tests are needed. If the D-dimer is high, a scan is needed. If the Wells score is moderate or high, the D-dimer is skipped and the person goes straight to a scan.

DVT can occur in an arm as well as a leg. Common features are pain or tenderness, swelling, warmth, redness or discolouration and swollen surface veins, although about half of people with the condition have no symptoms. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain.

sections.heading: How is a DVT treated?
sections.body:
Blood-thinning medicines (anticoagulants) are the main treatment. Current NHS advice favours tablets such as rivaroxaban or apixaban, although warfarin is also used. The NHS says people usually need to take them for at least three months to reduce the risk of another clot.

A Cambridge hospital leaflet gives more detail on length. For a first DVT with no clear cause, three to six months of treatment is usual, depending on the bleeding risk. For someone who has had a DVT before, staying on treatment for life is normally recommended.

Blood thinners do not dissolve the clot. The body absorbs it over time. The medicine stops it growing and helps prevent new clots. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are reserved for severe cases.

sections.heading: Living with blood thinners
sections.body:
All anticoagulants increase the risk of bleeding. A Cambridge hospital leaflet lists the signs that need prompt advice from a GP, NHS 111 or, in an emergency, 999: black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, coughing or vomiting blood, severe period bleeding, heavy or persistent nosebleeds and unexplained severe bruising.

The same leaflet says aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen or diclofenac should be avoided unless a GP advises otherwise, and that paracetamol is the painkiller generally used alongside anticoagulants. It also advises checking with a doctor before taking hormone replacement therapy or the combined contraceptive pill after a clot.

On travel, a Cambridge leaflet advises delaying flights or long journeys until at least two weeks after starting blood-thinning medicine. It adds that aspirin has not been shown to reduce the risk of clots on long journeys, and that anyone who develops leg pain or swelling, chest pain or breathlessness afterwards should seek medical advice.

sections.heading: What are the long-term effects of a DVT?
sections.body:
The most serious complication is a pulmonary embolism, in which a clot travels to the lungs. It can be life-threatening and needs to be treated quickly.

Post-thrombotic syndrome is the main long-term problem in the leg. Hospital leaflets describe chronic leg pain, swelling, redness and sometimes sores or ulcers. It usually develops within the first two years. Estimates of how many people are affected vary between sources, and it is more likely after extensive clots.

Compression stockings are a common way to manage the symptoms. A UCLH leaflet says they should not be worn until the initial leg swelling has settled, and another hospital leaflet notes that people with circulation or skin problems may not be able to use them. Some people who develop post-thrombotic syndrome are advised to wear them for more than two years.

The NHS advises avoiding long periods of sitting still, and walking around regularly or doing calf exercises.

sections.heading: Who is at risk of a DVT, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
A Cambridge hospital leaflet lists these risk factors: a clotting abnormality in the blood, including a family history, pregnancy, obesity, an underlying cancer, a previous DVT, immobility including long-haul flights, contraceptive pills, recent surgery and intravenous drug use. The NHS adds smoking, being over 60, taking hormone replacement therapy and having varicose veins.

A Black Country hospital leaflet says about one in 1,000 pregnant women have a DVT while pregnant or within about six weeks of giving birth. The same leaflet says warfarin is known to be harmful to a developing baby and that the effects of the newer direct oral anticoagulants in pregnancy are unknown, so anyone who is or may become pregnant should tell their doctor straight away so that a different anticoagulant can be prescribed. Injections of low-molecular-weight heparin are used instead.

In hospital, patients are assessed for their clot risk and may be given compression stockings or preventive medicine.

faqs.q: Does a blood thinner dissolve the clot?
faqs.a: No. A hospital leaflet says the blood thinner does not dissolve the clot and the body absorbs it over time. The medicine stops the clot growing and helps prevent new ones forming. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are kept for severe cases.

faqs.q: How long are blood thinners taken for?
faqs.a: The NHS says people usually need them for at least three months. A Cambridge leaflet says a first DVT with no clear cause is usually treated for three to six months, while a repeat DVT normally means treatment for life. The clinician sets the length.

faqs.q: Can I fly after a DVT?
faqs.a: A Cambridge hospital leaflet advises delaying flights or long journeys until at least two weeks after starting blood-thinning medicine. Anyone who develops leg pain or swelling, chest pain or breathlessness after a long journey should seek medical advice.

faqs.q: Can ibuprofen be taken with anticoagulants?
faqs.a: A Cambridge hospital leaflet says aspirin and anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen, naproxen or diclofenac should be avoided unless a GP advises otherwise, and that paracetamol is generally used instead. Anyone unsure should ask a pharmacist or GP.

faqs.q: When does a DVT become an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain, as this can mean the clot has reached the lungs. A swollen, painful leg alone needs a same-day medical assessment, with a scan within 24 hours.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
The NHS lists sudden breathlessness, chest pain that gets worse when breathing in and coughing up blood as the main symptoms, with leg pain or swelling also possible if a DVT is present. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or passing out.

Symptoms are not the same for everyone. Hospital leaflets note that some people have no symptoms at all, and that symptoms can also build up slowly over days to weeks rather than suddenly. For this reason a pulmonary embolism cannot be confirmed or ruled out from symptoms alone, and tests are needed.

sections.heading: What causes a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets say that in almost all cases the cause is a blood clot that formed in a deep vein, known as a DVT, usually in the leg or pelvis, and then travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from a clot in the heart.

The leaflets list similar risk factors. These include immobility, recent surgery or trauma and being in hospital; pregnancy and the period after delivery; oestrogen-containing contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy; cancer, obesity, smoking and older age; and a previous clot or a family history of clots. Some people have an inherited or acquired tendency for their blood to clot (thrombophilia).

Sometimes a pulmonary embolism happens for no obvious reason. Doctors describe these as unprovoked, and the likely cause is important in deciding how long treatment continues.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism diagnosed?
sections.body:
A Scottish NHS guideline describes a pathway that starts with a clinical probability score of low, intermediate or high, followed by a D-dimer blood test. The Whittington Health guideline says D-dimer is used to exclude the diagnosis in people at low risk, and that imaging is used to confirm it.

The usual confirming scan is a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), which also shows the state of the blood vessels in the lungs. A Gloucestershire hospital leaflet notes that the scan is rarely done on the first visit, so patients usually return for it. D-dimer is not infallible and can miss a clot.

The Scottish guideline says that while the diagnosis is unconfirmed, a full-strength dose of injected low-molecular-weight heparin or a tablet anticoagulant can be given. Treatment can therefore begin before the scan result is back.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism treated?
sections.body:
Once the diagnosis is confirmed, treatment usually continues with anticoagulant tablets or injections, depending on what suits the person. Anticoagulants do not dissolve the clot. The body clears it over time. They stop existing clots growing and help prevent new ones forming. Clot-busting drugs are reserved for severe cases.

Hospital leaflets say treatment can last anywhere from three months to the rest of a person's life, depending on the cause and the person's risk of another clot. The Whittington Health guideline says the likely cause of the clot is important for deciding how long to treat.

Anticoagulants raise the risk of bleeding. Anyone taking them who has black or bloody stools, vomits or coughs up blood, or has heavy or persistent bleeding should seek urgent medical advice from NHS 111, or call 999 in an emergency.

sections.heading: What is recovery from a pulmonary embolism like?
sections.body:
The NHS says a full recovery is expected if a pulmonary embolism is spotted and treated early. Hospital leaflets say breathlessness and tiredness are common and improve gradually, and that a return to normal can take several weeks to months. They advise seeing a GP if breathlessness on exertion persists beyond about eight weeks.

Some people have longer-term problems. One NHS leaflet notes that long-term complications, including breathlessness and heart problems, can follow a pulmonary embolism. This is called chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

The outlook is worse when a serious existing illness, such as advanced cancer, contributed to the clot. For most other people, treated promptly, the picture is much better. Questions about long-term treatment, travel or hormone medicines belong with the treating team or GP.

faqs.q: Where do the clots in a pulmonary embolism come from?
faqs.a: NHS hospital leaflets say that in almost all cases the clot formed in a deep vein, usually in the leg or pelvis, and travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from the heart.

faqs.q: Can a pulmonary embolism cause no symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. Hospital leaflets say some people have no symptoms, and that symptoms can build up slowly over days to weeks. Tests are needed to confirm or rule out the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Why is a D-dimer test not enough on its own?
faqs.a: A D-dimer is used to exclude a pulmonary embolism in people at low risk, not to confirm it. Imaging, usually a CT pulmonary angiogram, is used to confirm the diagnosis. D-dimer can also occasionally miss a clot.

faqs.q: How long does treatment last?
faqs.a: Hospital leaflets say it can last from three months to the rest of a person's life. The length depends on the cause of the clot and the risk of another one, and the treating team makes the decision.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take?
faqs.a: Breathlessness and tiredness are common and improve gradually. The NHS says people should make a full recovery if the condition is treated early, though a return to normal can take several weeks to months.

sections.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
sections.body:
Type 1 diabetes is a lifelong condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is an autoimmune condition: the immune system damages the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas. Without insulin the body cannot move glucose out of the blood and into cells, so regular insulin treatment is needed to keep glucose levels in a healthy range.

The NHS notes that the tendency can run in families. Researchers have not pinned down what sets off the autoimmune process, and research reviews have suggested that viral infections and other factors may play a part.

Type 1 is a different condition from type 2 diabetes, which accounts for the large majority of diabetes worldwide. The NHS lists the classic early signs as needing the toilet more, being thirsty, feeling tired and losing weight, often remembered as the four Ts. NIDDK notes that some people first find out they have type 1 diabetes when they develop signs of diabetic ketoacidosis.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP will usually test a urine sample and may check blood glucose, then send the person to hospital for assessment. The NHS says people usually stay in hospital until the blood test results are back, which is generally the same day.

The NHS says symptoms of type 1 diabetes can appear over a few days or weeks. The other signs it lists are blurred vision, sweet or fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections.

Because diabetic ketoacidosis can be the first sign, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms worsen quickly, or if stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing develop. A same-day GP appointment is the usual route for the earlier warning signs in a child or young person.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes treated day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment means taking insulin for life and regularly checking blood glucose. Most people take both a long-acting insulin, once or twice a day, and a rapid-acting insulin before meals. This pattern is known as basal-bolus treatment.

Insulin can be given with pens or by a pump, a device worn on the body that delivers small amounts of insulin through the day and night. Pump therapy can be used by adults, teenagers and children with adult supervision.

The amount of mealtime insulin varies with the blood glucose level before the meal and with the amount of carbohydrate eaten, which is why carbohydrate counting is taught. NHS inform lists the other ongoing tasks: checking glucose, recognising the signs of a hypo, attending check-ups and planning for driving and pregnancy.

One NHS 111 Wales page stresses that treatment should not be stopped during illness, and that the treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed.

sections.heading: What is a hypo?
sections.body:
A hypo is a lower-than-normal level of glucose in the blood. NICE lists dizziness, tiredness, hunger, shaking and sweating among the symptoms, and notes that some people with long-standing diabetes do not always spot the warning signs.

NHS inform says a hypo happens when injected insulin moves too much glucose out of the bloodstream. Common triggers include too much insulin, a skipped meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

Mild hypos are usually treated with something sugary. Severe ones may need an injection of glucagon into a muscle or glucose given into a vein.

NICE says the annual review should check that the person can recognise the symptoms of a hypo.

sections.heading: What is diabetic ketoacidosis?
sections.body:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs when a lack of insulin lets harmful substances called ketones build up in the blood. It can be life-threatening and needs urgent treatment in hospital. Diabetes UK lists thirst, passing urine more, stomach pain, sickness, deep breathing, fruity-smelling breath, tiredness or confusion and blurred vision. It says symptoms usually develop over about 24 hours but can be faster.

The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. People with type 1 diabetes are taught to test for ketones when they are unwell, and the NHS gives the blood and urine levels at which to ring 999, or at which to contact the diabetes team for advice.

Untreated, DKA can cause vomiting, dehydration, unconsciousness and death.

sections.heading: What are the long-term complications and checks?
sections.body:
Over time, high glucose can damage blood vessels and nerves. The NHS describes three main areas. In the eyes, damage to blood vessels can cause sight problems (diabetic retinopathy) and, uncommonly, blindness, so adults and children aged 12 or over are offered eye screening every year. In the feet, nerve damage means small cuts may go unnoticed and can become ulcers, so the NHS advises checking the feet every day and having a foot examination at least once a year. In the kidneys, damage usually causes no symptoms at first, so a test is advised every year.

NICE describes an annual review that covers foot checks, dental checks for gum disease and screening for kidney and nerve problems. Cholesterol and blood pressure are also checked, and blood pressure is checked in children too.

faqs.q: Is type 1 diabetes the same as type 2?
faqs.a: No. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so insulin is needed from diagnosis. Type 2 is a different condition and accounts for the great majority of diabetes worldwide.

faqs.q: What are the four Ts of type 1 diabetes?
faqs.a: The NHS lists needing the toilet more, thirst, tiredness and weight loss as the core signs, often remembered as the four Ts. Blurred vision, fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections can also occur.

faqs.q: Why do hypos happen?
faqs.a: NHS inform says a hypo happens when injected insulin moves too much glucose out of the blood. Common triggers include taking too much insulin, skipping a meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

faqs.q: Should insulin carry on during illness?
faqs.a: One NHS 111 Wales page says it is very important not to stop treatment when ill. The treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed, and the diabetes care team is the place to ask.

faqs.q: When is diabetic ketoacidosis an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. DKA can be life-threatening and needs urgent hospital treatment.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of ovarian cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a swollen tummy or feeling bloated as a main symptom, and says symptoms are the ones that happen frequently, roughly 12 or more times a month. Cancer Research UK adds a swollen or painful tummy, loss of appetite and changes in passing urine. Early-stage disease may cause no symptoms, and any that do occur tend to be very general.

The Royal Marsden notes that many of these symptoms overlap with other conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome and endometriosis. That is one reason a symptom on its own does not mean cancer.

The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms like these that are new, persistent or frequent for the person. A GP appointment is the usual first step, and the GP decides whether tests such as a CA125 blood test are needed.

sections.heading: Who is at risk of ovarian cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says the risk of ovarian cancer increases with age, and most cases in the UK are in women over 50. It lists an inherited faulty gene, such as the BRCA genes or those linked to Lynch syndrome, a previous breast or bowel cancer, previous radiotherapy, endometriosis, smoking and being overweight among the factors that raise risk.

The Royal Marsden notes that BRCA1 and BRCA2 are two genes known to be associated with an increased risk of both breast and ovarian cancer. Taking the combined contraceptive pill appears to reduce the risk. The same source says there is no concrete evidence that fertility treatment increases it.

Risk factors do not guarantee disease. Many people with several risk factors never develop ovarian cancer, and some people with none do.

sections.heading: How are the stage and type of ovarian cancer described?
sections.body:
Ovarian cancer is staged from 1 to 4. Cancer Research UK describes stage 1 as cancer found only in one or both ovaries, and stage 4 as cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body such as the liver or lungs. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look under the microscope. Stage and grade are used together to plan treatment and to judge the outlook.

There are different types. Target Ovarian Cancer describes high-grade serous cancer, which is the type PARP inhibitors are mainly used for, and low-grade serous cancer, for which a different group of targeted drugs, MEK inhibitors, are used.

MedlinePlus says survival depends strongly on stage at diagnosis and is better when the cancer is found before it spreads beyond the ovary. Cancer Research UK and other charities hold current national figures.

sections.heading: How is ovarian cancer treated?
sections.body:
The main treatments are surgery and chemotherapy. Surgery is usually the first step. In early ovarian cancer, surgery may be the only treatment needed, and chemotherapy afterwards aims to lower the risk of the cancer returning. In advanced disease, chemotherapy may be given before surgery, after it, or both. NHS inform says chemotherapy is sometimes given on its own as the main treatment if surgery is not possible. Radiotherapy is rarely used and is mainly for easing symptoms.

Target Ovarian Cancer describes targeted treatments. PARP inhibitors are offered to people with stage 3 or 4 high-grade epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer that has responded to platinum-based chemotherapy, and can usually only be accessed once. Bevacizumab is available whether or not someone has a BRCA variant.

The Royal Marsden notes that people with the same type of cancer may have different treatment plans, which a specialist team agrees with them.

sections.heading: Life after treatment for ovarian cancer
sections.body:
NHS inform says that anyone who has not yet been through the menopause will usually be brought into it by treatment. Cancer and its treatment can cause physical and emotional changes that affect a person's sex life, and difficulties usually slowly improve after treatment.

Follow-up involves regular check-ups. CA125 blood tests are sometimes done as part of follow-up, and a rising level may be a sign that the cancer has returned. Ovarian cancer can come back, and a person who notices new symptoms, or symptoms they had before returning, is advised to contact their specialist doctor or nurse.

Specialist nurses can offer support, and Macmillan Cancer Support has information on coping with advanced cancer. The NHS says a person with ovarian cancer can get support from their specialist team and from charities.

faqs.q: How is ovarian cancer diagnosed?
faqs.a: A blood test and a scan are usually the first tests. CA125 is a blood marker that is often raised in ovarian cancer, and imaging is typically an ultrasound or CT scan. Tissue from a biopsy or from surgery is examined under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Do bloating and tummy pain mean ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: Not usually. The Royal Marsden notes these symptoms overlap with other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and endometriosis. The NHS advises seeing a GP if they are new, persistent or frequent, so the cause can be looked into.

faqs.q: Will treatment bring on the menopause?
faqs.a: NHS inform says that if the person has not already been through the menopause, treatment will usually cause it. The specialist team can explain the effects and the options for managing them.

faqs.q: What are PARP inhibitors?
faqs.a: They are targeted drugs. Target Ovarian Cancer says they are offered to people with stage 3 or 4 high-grade epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer that has responded to platinum-based chemotherapy, and can usually only be accessed once.

faqs.q: Can ovarian cancer come back?
faqs.a: Yes. NHS inform says ovarian cancer can return, and follow-up check-ups look out for this. A person who notices new symptoms, or old ones returning, is advised to contact their specialist doctor or nurse.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of cervical cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS lists unusual vaginal bleeding, including bleeding during or after sex, between periods or after the menopause, as the main symptom. Other symptoms are changes in vaginal discharge, pain during sex, and pelvic or lower back pain.

Early cervical cancer often causes no symptoms, so the NHS says that symptoms appearing between regular screening appointments should not wait for the next one. A GP appointment is the route: the NHS advises being checked if symptoms change, get worse or do not feel normal for the person.

Cancer Research UK notes that these symptoms are common and have many other causes, so they do not confirm cancer. Screening cannot assess symptoms. The usual next steps are an examination and, if needed, referral for a closer look at the cervix.

sections.heading: What causes cervical cancer?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales says nearly all cervical cancers are linked to infection with certain high-risk types of the human papillomavirus (HPV). A Newcastle hospitals leaflet adds that HPV is very common and that most people clear the virus without problems.

Two measures target this chain of events. All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine, and everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular cervical screening. This includes women and anyone else who has a cervix. Screening looks for HPV and abnormal cells before cancer develops.

Screening is a way of finding changes early. It is not a diagnostic test for cancer, and one source notes that Pap smears screen for, but do not diagnose, cervical pre-cancers.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis often begins with an abnormal screening result. Colposcopy is usually the first step after one: the cervix is looked at closely, and a small punch biopsy is common. A loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy can also give tissue to examine. Colposcopy does not establish a diagnosis of cancer on its own. A biopsy does.

NHS inform notes that cancer is found in only a very small share of the people referred for colposcopy.

If cancer is found, tests such as an MRI scan, a PET-CT scan or a chest X-ray may be used to see how far it has spread. Doctors describe this as the stage, using the FIGO system, which has four stages numbered 1 to 4 based on the size of the cancer and whether it has spread.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer treated?
sections.body:
Treatment usually includes surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and depends on the size and type of the cancer and where it is. Surgery is the main treatment for early disease, and the types include LLETZ, cone biopsy, hysterectomy and trachelectomy. Radiotherapy may be used instead of surgery for someone not fit for a big operation or general anaesthetic, or after surgery to reduce the risk of the cancer coming back.

Cancer Research UK says chemotherapy can be given at the same time as radiotherapy, called chemoradiotherapy, for stage 1B2 to stage 4A cervical cancer, and that cisplatin is the most common drug. For stage 2, chemoradiotherapy is the main treatment, sometimes with surgery. In stage 4A a few people may be offered a pelvic exenteration, a major operation.

For cancer that has spread, treatment can include the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab with chemotherapy, with or without the targeted drug bevacizumab. Small cell cancer of the cervix is rare and is treated differently.

sections.heading: Fertility and support
sections.body:
The specialist care team will talk about the effect treatment may have on fertility. If fertility cannot be preserved through the treatment itself, a doctor can refer the person to a fertility specialist. Options such as storing eggs or embryos before treatment can be discussed. Trachelectomy is one operation designed for people who wish to keep the option of pregnancy.

The NHS says people with cervical cancer can get support from their specialist team and from charities such as Macmillan Cancer Support. Cancer Research UK notes that coping with a cancer diagnosis can be difficult, both practically and emotionally.

Prognosis depends on the type of cancer, its stage and whether it comes back after treatment. MedlinePlus says the five-year survival rate falls as the cancer spreads outside the walls of the cervix into other areas, which is why finding and treating it early matters.

faqs.q: Does an abnormal screening result mean cancer?
faqs.a: No. An abnormal result leads to colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix. NHS inform notes that cancer is found in only a very small share of the people referred. Most abnormal results lead to treatment of cell changes, not cancer.

faqs.q: What happens at colposcopy?
faqs.a: The cervix is examined closely, and a small punch biopsy is common. Tissue can also be taken with a loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy. Colposcopy is usually the first step after an abnormal screening result.

faqs.q: Does bleeding after sex mean cervical cancer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Cancer Research UK notes that these symptoms are common and have many other causes. The NHS still advises seeing a GP about unusual bleeding, because it needs to be checked and cannot be assessed by screening.

faqs.q: Can I still have children after treatment?
faqs.a: It depends on the treatment. The NHS says the specialist team will talk about the effect on fertility, and can refer to a fertility specialist. Egg or embryo storage before treatment can be discussed, and trachelectomy is an operation that aims to preserve fertility.

faqs.q: Who is invited for cervical screening?
faqs.a: The NHS says everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular screening. All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of PCOS?
sections.body:
Irregular or infrequent periods, extra hair on the face or body (hirsutism) and difficulty getting pregnant are among the most commonly listed signs. Acne, oily skin, weight gain, particularly around the waist, and thinning scalp hair also appear on some lists.

The NHS says infertility in PCOS is mainly due to a failure of ovulation. NHS 111 Wales lists less common symptoms: tiredness, depression, hair loss, miscarriage, pelvic pain and mood swings.

Symptoms vary a lot. NHS hospital leaflets say some women have mild symptoms, while others are affected more severely by a wider range of symptoms. NHS inform now titles its page on the condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), a name that reflects the hormonal and metabolic features of the condition.

sections.heading: How is PCOS diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a diagnosis can usually be made if other rare causes of the same symptoms have been ruled out and at least two of three criteria are met: irregular or infrequent periods, signs of excess male hormones, and polycystic-looking ovaries on a scan. Diagnosis usually involves hormone and blood tests to rule out other hormone-related conditions, and sometimes an ultrasound scan.

Having polycystic-looking ovaries on a scan is not enough by itself. A hospital leaflet says that around six or seven in 100 women with polycystic ovaries have PCOS, and that polycystic ovaries by themselves do not need treatment.

Diagnosis can be difficult because signs can come and go. A 2025 report by the all-party parliamentary group on PCOS says many people remain undiagnosed. A GP appointment is the usual first step for anyone with irregular periods or other symptoms.

sections.heading: How is PCOS treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for PCOS, but the symptoms can be treated. NHS 111 Wales advises that losing weight and eating a healthy, balanced diet can make some symptoms better for people who are overweight.

A Manchester NHS trust document lists the combined pill as the first-choice treatment for irregular bleeding, with metformin also listed for features such as excess hair and acne. Medicines are also available for excess hair growth and for fertility problems.

The choice depends on which symptoms matter most to the person, and the GP or specialist advises on it. The same document says that, where body mass index is raised, a weight loss of 5 to 10 per cent is encouraged with referral to a dietitian.

sections.heading: PCOS and fertility
sections.body:
PCOS can disrupt ovulation, which can make it harder to conceive. Fertility treatment can help some women to get a regular cycle and improves their chances of pregnancy.

NHS 111 Wales says clomifene is usually the first treatment recommended for women trying to conceive. If medicines do not work, in vitro fertilisation (IVF) may be offered, and a simple surgical procedure called laparoscopic ovarian drilling may be recommended. The NHS says that with treatment, most women with PCOS are able to get pregnant.

PCOS is also linked with a higher risk of pregnancy complications, such as high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and miscarriage, according to NHS pathway documents. Anyone planning a pregnancy is advised to talk to their GP or a fertility specialist.

sections.heading: PCOS, long-term health and mood
sections.body:
A North East London NHS pathway advises counselling about possible long-term complications, which include type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and cancer of the womb lining (endometrial cancer). Infrequent or absent periods are a risk factor for thickening of the womb lining. One NHS leaflet says PCOS does not increase the chance of breast, cervical or ovarian cancer. Getting symptoms under control earlier may help reduce the long-term risks.

Mental health matters too. Fertility problems and visible symptoms can cause distress and lower self-esteem. The 2025 all-party group report says mental health should be built into treatment, and that low mood and anxiety are among the effects. NHS pathways say screening for and managing mental health conditions is essential.

Many women manage their symptoms and long-term risks well, often without medication.

faqs.q: Can I get pregnant with PCOS?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The NHS says that with treatment most women with PCOS are able to get pregnant. PCOS can disrupt ovulation, so it can take longer. Clomifene is usually the first treatment, and IVF may be offered if medicines do not work.

faqs.q: Does having polycystic ovaries on a scan mean I have PCOS?
faqs.a: No. A hospital leaflet says only around six or seven in 100 women with polycystic ovaries have PCOS, and polycystic ovaries by themselves do not need treatment. Diagnosis needs at least two of three criteria.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for PCOS?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure, but the symptoms can be treated. Weight loss and a healthy diet can improve some symptoms, and medicines are available for irregular periods, excess hair and fertility problems.

faqs.q: Does PCOS raise the risk of type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: NHS pathway documents list type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and endometrial cancer as possible long-term complications. Getting symptoms under control earlier may help reduce these risks.

faqs.q: Can PCOS affect mental health?
faqs.a: Fertility problems and visible symptoms can cause distress and lower self-esteem. A 2025 all-party parliamentary group report says low mood and anxiety are among the effects, and NHS pathways say screening for and managing mental health conditions is essential.
